There have been a lot of conversations about the topic of being back to the office, and it looks like the general trend in most companies is to <a href="https://www.resumebuilder.com/9-in-10-companies-will-require-employees-to-work-from-office-in-2023/" alt="9 in 10 companies will require employees to work from office in 2023" target="_blank">make a 180-degree turn from pandemic times</a> and work slowly towards going back to the office.

Both options have several benefits and inconveniences, and I am sure everyone has explored some of them at some point in time. Let's state some obvious stuff beforehand: 

> _Obviously, these arguments are generalizations; everyone has a very specific set of circumstances._

# Distance
Distance is a problem; distance sucks. There is a reason why long-distance relationships are really challenging. Some would argue that they just don't work. It is obvious that in-person relationships are better overall.

Your relationship with your peers is better in person than through Teams. **Point office.**

# Work-life balance
This is really hard to match. If you have to take care of someone at home (kids, elders, etc…), working from home is definitely the way to go. **Point home.**

# Connection
Someone from the office recommended me the book <a href="https://thelostconnections.com" alt="Lost Connections by Johann Hari" target="_blank">Lost Connections by Johann Hari</a>, talking about anxiety and depression, real pandemics of our time. The book offers a very peculiar take on the role that 'human connections' play when dealing with these problems.

In this book, Johann Hari challenges the traditional understanding of depression and anxiety as solely a chemical imbalance and explores the profound impact of societal factors. He argues that depression and anxiety are often a response to disconnections from meaningful work, relationships, and nature. By uncovering and addressing these lost connections, we can find unexpected solutions to depression and improve mental well-being.

Take a look at this book if you want to know how sometimes a cow can be an antidepressant. 

Yes, a cow.

**Disclaimer:** _'Lost Connections' received both praise and criticism. Supporters appreciated its exploration of the broader societal factors impacting mental health and its call for a more holistic approach to treatment. Critics, on the other hand, raised concerns about some of the scientific claims made in the book and questioned the comprehensiveness of its analysis._

The point that I am trying to make is: **connecting with others is really important.**

There is something special going on when brilliant people are in the same room. Nobody can deny that. The creativity is better, the ideas bounce around easier, and the productivity is higher. **Point office.**

# Flexible hours
Flexible hours while working from home are truly flexible. Asynchronous work really benefits from the fact that you are in your own space.

In my case, I sometimes like working a couple of hours before going to sleep. In summertime, for example, when it's really hot, I like to wake up really early when everyone else is still sleeping and work a couple of hours as the sun is rising. With the window opened, the morning breeze is quite nice.

Obviously, you can do that if your work is asynchronous; you cannot expect other members of your team to be available at all times. Besides that, **Point home.**

# Working in your pyjamas

Are your kidding me? **POINT OFFICE!**

Seriously, there is no need to dress like you are going to a wedding when working from home, but clothes ARE important. <a href="https://www.smh.com.au/lifestyle/fashion-and-mood-how-clothes-affect-your-emotions-20150717-giei1f.html" alt="Fashion and mood: How clothes affect your emotions" target="_blank">They really affect your mood.</a>

Baggy clothes and big sweatshirts are related to depression, while dresses and jewelry are associated more with a happy or positive state of mind. Colors also influence the way we behave. For example, sports teams wearing all black are deemed to be more aggressive.

Just dress as you would when going to the office; it sets you in the correct state of mind for a productive day.

Spending the majority of your time at home can have negative effects on your mood, especially if you live alone (and have lots of cats).

![Grumpy cat](/assets/images/backToTheOffice/cat-kitty.gif#postImageSmall)

# When objective arguments are not enough

We could go on and on pointing out benefits and inconvenients of working from home or working at the office. Looks like we are on a situation where you can find numerous valid points for both sides of the argument. What do we do then, flip a coin?

Let’s see what our beloved collective mind has to say about it:

![ChatGPT](/assets/images/backToTheOffice/chatGPT.png#postImageBig)

That is crappy answer. I mean, it's true... but not very helpful. It sounds like a cheap therapist fresh from collegue. So, if we can't rely in our AI gods, how can we solve the problem?

# Circumstances

Each and every one of us is a unique world, a unique universe. Your circumstances are unique, and so are mine.

In my case, what I love about working from home is the ability to reconcile my family life, specifically being able to spend a lot of time with my kids. But I also really enjoy working in the office, connecting with my peers, drawing on whiteboards, and experiencing the heightened productivity that comes with being together.

Is there a way to fulfill all my desires? I would like to be able to take the kids to school in the morning and also be available for their extracurricular activities in the evening, such as soccer, dance, piano lessons, etc. However, with my commute, that is not possible. The math just doesn't work.

I've got it! Is there a way we can move the office right across the street from my home? Come on, it's a nice place...

Pretty please?

No?

# When reason comes at the door, dreams jump out of the window
At some point, we have to conduct a reality check and see if what we are asking for is actually reasonable.

My point is... all of you guys are _right_. Both the people arguing for working from home and those arguing for returning to the office have valid points. But now what... what is the value of _being right?_ I have never received a raise for _being right_, never won any prizes... nothing.

Being right is useless, so I stopped fighting that battle a long time ago. The infamous battle of egos.

However, we still need to find a solution. Better said **_build_** rather than _find_ a solution. Let's utilize our famous ingenuity to figure this one out.

There's one crucial question that I believe we need to be honest about:

- **What is best for the business?**

Take a moment to ponder it, consider your circumstances, and arrive at your own conclusion.
